title: Vettem vagy megvettem? Buying Something Specific

sections.title: vettem vs. megvettem
sections.content: You already know that the past tense agrees with its object the same way the present tense does: an unspecified object takes the indefinite ending, a specific one (marked by a, az, a possessive, or a name) takes the definite ending. vesz ("to buy") is irregular in the past — both endings attach to the same shortened stem vett-. Vettem egy kabátot. means "I bought a coat" (some coat, indefinite). Megvettem a kabátot. means "I bought the coat" (that one, definite) — and here the verb prefix meg- from Unit 22 is doing real work: at (én), indefinite and definite vettem are the exact same word, so meg- is what actually signals "the specific one" until the endings themselves start differing from (te) onward.

sections.title: Same object, two ways
rows: I bought the gift. (the one we talked about)

items.english: Yesterday I bought a nice coat.

items.spanish: Végül megvettem a kabátot, amit a kirakatban láttam.
items.english: In the end I bought the coat I saw in the shop window.

items.spanish: Károly megvette a jegyeket a moziba.
items.english: Károly bought the tickets for the movies.

sections.content: Not every definite past verb needs meg- — látta and találta stand on their own. meg- shows up specifically with vesz (and its suppletive relatives) because their 1sg form doesn't otherwise show indefinite vs. definite at all.
